evidence: Draft: 'Here is a little script you could use:'. Source (the working copy's line he approved; his published guide had 'For anxiety:'; his=false): 'A script you could use for anxiety is:'. PRESERVATION, word by word: 'script you could use' and the closing colon are kept, so the offer ('could'), the agent ('you') and the strength are unchanged; 'A ... is:' became 'Here is a ...', a presentational frame only. Two differences. (1) 'for anxiety' is no longer in the sentence. The change says the heading carries it, and CONTEXT.txt confirms that: the line directly above the draft is the heading 'Anxiety script', so the section still tells the reader the script is for anxiety and the sentence says nothing that conflicts with it. The change does not claim to put 'for anxiety' back, so nothing it promises is missing. (2) 'little' is new: a casual size word for a three-paragraph script of roughly 125 words. It adds no claim, condition, person or number and does not soften 'could use'. Nothing else is added and nothing else of the source is left out. The draft occurs once in CONTEXT.txt (line 3) and the section reads right: heading, lead-in, then the script's first-person lines. TELL ROWS: I checked T01-T29 and C01-C04 against the draft in its context. PRESENT: T19 (announcing setup). The sentence's only job is to announce the script that follows, so the writer's ABSENT on T19 ('does not announce what comes next') is wrong. Justified: the replaced line and his published 'For anxiety:' do the same job, the colon leads into text the reader is meant to say to themselves, and without this line the first-person script has no frame and the 'you could use' offer is lost; the change adds no announcer the source lacked. Borderline, judged ABSENT: T11 (generic bridge). Without 'for anxiety' the line could introduce any script, but the heading directly above gives it its topic and the line is needed to frame the script, so it is not connective tissue. Not present: T25 (the colon opens a real script, not a reveal); T26 ('little' returns two paragraphs later in 'little one', but 'a little script' is a common softener, not a distinctive repeated word, and 'script' repeating the heading is as in the source line); T22 and T10 (one offer, as in the source, with no reassurance and no permission formula); T14 (nothing has gone missing, 'anxiety' stays in the heading); T15 (the structure changed and the words are plain, not rarer synonyms); the rest, because this is an eight-word lead-in with no image, list, contrast, closer or first-person fact; C01 (no naming), C02 ('Here' points forward to the script just below), C03 and C04 (no fact or claim). I could not see other sections, so whether other scripts reuse this lead-in (T26 across the article) is not judged. LINTER: B7 short landing at paragraph end ('Here is a little script you could use:') is not a real problem here: the line is a whole paragraph that ends on a colon and hands on to the script paragraphs, it is not a closing line; accepted. D9 follows the source order (1/1): one eight-word line replacing one eight-word line, so there is no order to keep or break and T13/T09 have nothing to act on; accepted. E36/E41 heavy second person (12.5 'you' per 100 of the draft's words): one 'you' in eight words, the same count and density as the source line, and it is the offer itself ('you could use'); accepted.
